title: Tool / function calling
summary: Give an LLM typed tools it can call, run them in your code, and feed the results back to finish the task.
objectives: Explain why tool calling lets an LLM act, not just talk
Define a tool with a name, description, and JSON Schema input
Pass tools to the Claude Messages API and read a tool_use block
Execute the requested tool in your own code and return a tool_result
Loop on the stop_reason until Claude finishes (the agentic loop)
Handle tool errors and force a specific tool with tool_choice

quiz.q: In tool calling, who actually runs the tool's code?
quiz.why: For user-defined tools the model only requests the call; your code executes it and returns the result. (Server-side tools like web search are the exception.)

quiz.q: What field tells you Claude wants to call a tool instead of finishing?
quiz.why: When response.stop_reason is "tool_use", the content contains a tool_use block you must execute and respond to.

quiz.q: What does a tool definition need at minimum?
quiz.answer: A name, a description, and an input_schema (JSON Schema describing the inputs).
quiz.why: Claude reads the description and schema to decide when to call the tool and how to shape the arguments.

quiz.q: When you send a tool result back, what must it reference?
quiz.why: Each tool_result must carry the same tool_use_id as the tool_use block, so Claude pairs the answer with its request.

quiz.q: How do you signal that a tool call failed?
quiz.answer: Return the tool_result with is_error set to true and an informative message.
quiz.why: Claude sees the error and can retry differently or ask for clarification instead of assuming success.

quiz.q: Why parse tool inputs with json.loads rather than string matching?
options: Escaping can vary, so only a real JSON parse is reliable
quiz.why: Models may escape Unicode or slashes differently in the input field; parse the JSON instead of matching raw text.

body_markdown:
## Why tool calling?

An LLM on its own can only produce text. It cannot look up today's weather, query your database, or send an email. **Tool calling** (also called **function calling**) closes that gap: you describe some functions to the model, and when it needs one, it asks you to run it and tell it the result.

Think of it like a function in maths. You hand the model a signature - a name and the shape of its inputs - and it decides *when* to call it and *with what arguments*. Your code computes the output and hands it back.

## How the conversation flows

The key idea: **the model never runs your code**. It only *requests* a call. The loop is:

1. You send a message plus a list of tools.
2. Claude replies. If `stop_reason` is `"tool_use"`, the reply contains a `tool_use` block with a tool name and JSON inputs.
3. Your code runs that tool and sends back a `tool_result` with the matching `tool_use_id`.
4. Claude reads the result and either answers or calls another tool. You repeat until `stop_reason` is `"end_turn"`.

## Defining a tool

A tool is a **name**, a **description**, and an **input_schema** written as JSON Schema. The description matters a lot - Claude uses it to decide when the tool applies, so say *when* to call it, not just what it does.

```python
weather_tool = {
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Get the current weather for a city. Call this whenever the user asks about weather.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "city": {"type": "string", "description": "City name, e.g. London"}
        },
        "required": ["city"],
    },
}
```

## The agentic loop

Here is the full round trip with the Claude Messages API. We keep looping until Claude stops asking for tools.

```python
import json
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

def get_weather(city):
    return f"18 degrees and cloudy in {city}"

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in London?"}]

while True:
    resp = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        tools=[weather_tool],
        messages=messages,
    )
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    results = []
    for block in resp.content:
        if block.type == "tool_use":
            out = get_weather(**block.input)  # block.input is already parsed JSON
            results.append({
                "type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": block.id,
                "content": out,
            })
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

print(next(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text"))
```

## Errors and forcing a tool

If a tool fails, do not crash - return the result with `is_error` set to `true` and a clear message, so Claude can adapt. And if you need to *guarantee* a specific tool gets used, set `tool_choice`.

```python
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=[weather_tool],
    tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "get_weather"},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "London weather?"}],
)
```

## Your task

Write a tool called `calculate` that takes a maths expression and returns the answer, wire it into the loop above, and ask Claude a word problem that forces it to call your tool.

slides.title: Tool / function calling
slides.narration: Welcome back. So far our language model can only produce text. In this lesson we give it hands. Tool calling, also called function calling, lets the model ask your code to run a function and use the result. By the end you'll be able to define a tool, pass it to the Claude A P I, run the tool yourself, and feed the answer back so the model can finish the job.

slides.title: Why tool calling?
bullets: An L L M alone can only output text.
It can't fetch data or take actions.
Tools let it call your functions.
Like a function: inputs in, output out.
slides.narration: On its own, a language model can only write text. It can't look up today's weather, query your database, or send an email. Tool calling closes that gap. You describe some functions, and when the model needs one, it asks you to run it. As a maths graduate this will feel familiar: you give it a function signature, and it decides when to call it and with what inputs.

slides.title: The model never runs your code
bullets: The model only REQUESTS a call.
slides.narration: Here's the most important idea, and the one beginners miss. The model never runs your code. It only requests a call, naming a tool and the arguments. Your own application executes that function and returns the result. The model is the decision-maker; you are the executor. There are some Anthropic-hosted server-side tools that run for you, like web search, but user-defined tools always run in your code.

slides.title: Defining a tool
bullets: A name, a description, an input_schema.
Say WHEN to call it, not just what.
slides.narration: A tool is three things: a name, a description, and an input schema written in Jason Schema. The description carries real weight, because the model reads it to decide when the tool applies. So be prescriptive: say when to call it, not only what it does. The schema describes the arguments, here a single required string called city.

slides.title: Passing tools to the A P I
bullets: Use the Claude Messages A P I.
Keep your key in an env var.
slides.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=[weather_tool],
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Weather in London?"}],
)
slides.narration: To use a tool, you pass a list of tools into the messages dot create call on the Claude Messages A P I. Notice we never hard-code the A P I key; the client reads it from the environment variable ANTHROPIC underscore A P I underscore KEY. Here we ask about the weather in London and offer the get underscore weather tool.

slides.title: Reading a tool_use block
bullets: Find the tool_use block in content.
slides.narration: When the model wants a tool, the response's stop reason is the string tool underscore use. Inside the content you'll find a block whose type is tool underscore use, carrying the tool name and the inputs. The S D K gives you block dot input already parsed as a dictionary, so you don't parse the Jason yourself. Always rely on that parsed object rather than matching raw text.

slides.title: Returning a tool_result
bullets: Run the tool in your code.
slides.code:
out = get_weather(**block.input)
results.append({
    "type": "tool_result",
    "tool_use_id": block.id,
    "content": out,
})
messages.append({"role": "user",
                 "content": results})
slides.narration: Now you execute the function and send the answer back. The result block has type tool underscore result, and it must carry the same tool underscore use underscore id that came in the request. That id is how the model pairs your answer with the call it made. You append these results as a new user message and send the conversation again.

slides.title: The agentic loop
slides.code:
while True:
    resp = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024, tools=[weather_tool],
        messages=messages)
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    # ... run tools, append results ...
slides.narration: Put it together and you get the agentic loop. You keep calling the A P I as long as the stop reason is tool use. Each time, you append the model's reply, run the requested tools, append the results, and go round again. When the stop reason becomes end underscore turn, the model is finished and you read its final text answer. That loop is the heart of every tool-using agent.

slides.title: Errors and forcing a tool
bullets: On failure: is_error true plus a message.
Don't crash; let the model adapt.
slides.narration: Things go wrong, so handle it gracefully. If a tool fails, don't crash. Return the result with is underscore error set to true and a clear message; the model will see it and either try again differently or ask for help. And when you must guarantee a particular tool runs, set tool underscore choice to that tool by name. Both give you control over an otherwise free-roaming model.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Model requests; your code runs it.
slides.narration: Let's recap. A tool is a name, a description, and a Jason Schema for its inputs. The model only requests a call; your code runs the function and returns a tool result carrying the matching id. You loop until the stop reason is end turn, and you handle errors by flagging them rather than crashing. Your task before the next lesson: write a calculate tool that evaluates a maths expression, wire it into the loop, and pose a word problem that forces the model to call it. See you next time.
